::: {.callout-note}
MaxwellBloch is now **clerq**. See [what changed and how to update](news/rename.qmd).
:::

clerq solves the propagation of classical electromagnetic fields through media
of open quantum systems, using Maxwell's equations coupled to the Lindblad
master equation. It is used for near-resonant light in thermal atomic vapours,
with two-, three- and many-level atoms, spontaneous decay, dephasing and
Doppler broadening.

![Propagation of a 4π pulse through a dense atomic vapour. The pulse
immediately breaks up on entering the medium and the resultant pulses form two
optical solitons each with a pulse area of 2π.](example.gif)

clerq is used for theoretical research, for modelling experiments and for
undergraduate and graduate teaching. It can model two, three or many-level
systems with physical effects including:

* Inhomogeneous broadening due to spontaneous decay,
* Doppler broadening in thermal systems,
* Collision dephasing,
* Sub-level structure.

Modules are also available for:

* Generating hyperfine structure for alkali atoms with the correct channels and
  angular momentum factors for coupling and decay,
* Spectral analysis,
* Plotting and animating solutions.

Some phenomena that can be demonstrated:

* Linear absorption and dispersion,
* Fast light and slow light,
* Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT),
* Storage and retrieval of light pulses,
* Self-Induced Transparency (SIT) and optical solitons,
* Matched pulses and simultons,
* Hyperfine pumping.

See the [Examples](examples/index.qmd) for details.

## Source code

clerq is open source. The code, issue tracker and releases are on GitHub:
**[github.com/tpogden/clerq](https://github.com/tpogden/clerq)**.
